history.content: My sorghum is not growing well and I see tiny pink flowers at the base, what can I do?

draws.answer: The problem is maize streak virus on your sorghum, not streak virus on your sorghum. First, walk through your sorghum field and look for chlorotic spots that turn into broken, water-soaked streaks along the veins and any plants with dead-heart symptoms. Then pull out and destroy the most badly affected sorghum plants to remove the source of the virus. For the following season, choose a sorghum variety that is resistant to maize streak virus. Ask ICAT for the appropriate variety.

Those tiny pink flowers are a sign of thrips, so you need to act fast. Spray an approved insecticide at the labelled rate to control the thrips. After the spray, go through the field again and count the flowers on the underside of the leaves. If the count is high, you should pick the most infested leaves and destroy them, and also clear the weeds around the plot edges. Use a resistant sorghum variety for the next season. history.content: My cassava plants have yellow stripes on the leaf veins and the roots feel hard and brown when I pull them up. Is this brown streak disease?

draws.answer: It is cassava mosaic disease, not brown streak disease. When you plant again, cut only from healthy-looking cassava plants with normal green leaves and no deformation. Use an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. To obtain clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

history.content: My herd of goats and sheep shows fever, muco-purulent discharge from nose and eyes, and many are dying quickly, what should I do?

draws.answer: This is a tick-borne disease of your goats and sheep: gall sickness, caused by Anaplasma marginale. Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can confirm it is gall sickness and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine - red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animals in the shade, give clean water and do not make them walk. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick animals. Never reuse a needle between animals. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

Fever, noisy breathing and rapid death in many animals point to Newcastle disease in your goats and sheep. First isolate every surviving animal from the sick ones and do not move, sell or give away any goat or sheep. Then burn or bury the dead animals and the soiled litter and disinfect the pen thoroughly. After the pen is disinfected, vaccinate the entire herd with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, and repeat the vaccination on the recommended schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary without delay.

history.content: My sorghum plants stay short and yellow even though the rains are good, what is happening?

draws.answer: Your sorghum is suffering from nitrogen shortage in a run-down soil. First, look at the leaves: the uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves tells you the plant is lacking nitrogen, not that it has a disease. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word because mineral fertilizer alone often does not work on depleted soil. Bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Next, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot.

history.content: purple weed at sorghum base

draws.answer: The purple weed, called Striga, is pulled from the field before the sorghum flowers. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing 3 to 5 seeds per pocket at 3 to 5 centimetres depth and using 3 to 5 kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Two to three weeks after sowing, perform the first weeding without breaking the ridges. Then apply the Striga pull at the tillering stage, which is when the plants are 30 to 45 days old. If you need help matching the sorghum variety to the best Striga tolerance, see ICAT or ITRA.

Use a resistant variety that matures in 55 to 75 days. Choose a cycle of 75 to 85 days when rains are strong, such as June-July in Maritime/Plateaux or March-April in Centrale/Kara/Savanes. Sow when the rains are strong, from mid-June to early July in Maritime/Plateaux or from mid-March to early April in Centrale/Kara/Savanes. Weed at 15 to 25 days after sowing. Avoid over-applying nitrogen; split urea and not exceeding the recommended dose. For a fit variety, go to ICAT.

The purple-flowered weed you see is chili pepper, likely Solanella sudamelia, also called groundnut or strawberry thistle. First, pull out and destroy the plants that host the chili pepper early in the season to stop them spreading. Second, sow your sorghum early and at the recommended close spacing, because dense a seedlings early will suffer less. Third, keep the sorghum field weed-free to reduce the number of chili pepper habitats. If you need help with the early weeding or any other issues, contact ICAT.

history.content: How do I manage an outbreak of peste des petits ruminants in my goats?

draws.answer: Peste des petits ruminants is called leucaena poisoning when the rumen is over-sourced with leucaena. Reduce leucaena to at most a quarter to a third of the ration and never let it be the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen plenty of roughage. Introduce any feed change gradually over several days. Keep a continuous supply of clean water and a mineral or salt source. If appetite does not recover, or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, call the veterinary service. I cannot give you a specific date for when this outbreak starts.

The disease is called bloat. First, get the goat up and moving while keeping its head raised to help it belch the gas. Next, drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth so gas can escape. Call the veterinary service immediately because severe cases need their intervention without delay. The veterinary service is the only one who can do this safely.

After harvesting, either drop a pinch of the neem powder into each funnel or bury the whole stalk with the soil, and avoid eating the plants. history.content: My sorghum is getting tiny and I see a pink weed at the stem, how do I stop it?

draws.answer: The problem is stem borer on sorghum, and you must use three stages of neem oil. First, spray a weak solution of neem oil on the whole field, following the label rate. Then wait ten days and apply the second, stronger spray at that same rate. After the second spray, wait another ten days and apply the third spray. Always make sure you use a canary or other flame-free container because the oil can ignite. After each spray, go to ICAT to confirm the pest is still present. You need to rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source. For the next season, ask ICAT for a tolerant variety. I cannot give you an exact dosage without seeing the field.

First, sow your groundnut, soya or cowpea early and at the recommended close spacing to give the young plants a good start. Keep the field weed-free at two weeks after sowing and again about thirty days after the seed is in the soil, because weeds and aphids live there between crops. Remember that Pappé affects cattle, sheep and goats, so focus on the animal health of your herd rather than selling. The veterinary service will guide you on containment and next steps.

Keep all visitors away from the pen. Disinfect the pen, install a footbath at the entrance, and boil any food scraps before feeding. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: Is it okay to mix two different insecticides for a more potent spray?

draws.answer: No, and you should not make a stronger mix. The guidance treats the spray as a product and gives a dose per kilogram for each one, so a mixed dose is not one dose more; the active ingredient in each container is what makes the product strong. What makes it stronger is the combination, not the strength of the ingredient: an insect that dies from more than one thing is not the pest anymore.

No, and there is no safer mix. Mixing two products is mixing diseases, and there is no cure once a virus infects. What you can do safely: separate the affected plants, keep visitors away, destroy them, and clean the plot. Then scout for whiteflies and aphids regularly, use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies, and spray a strong jet of water on aphids, letting ladyhaws and lacewings help. If the attack is heavy, ICAT can tell you which product is approved and how to use it.

history.content: how much urea should I add to soil for Striga control

draws.answer: You should use a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay for each funnel on young plants, about 1 kg per hectare, which is roughly the amount needed for Striga control. Apply this mixture into each funnel and repeat the application every 8-10 days while the crop is still young. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always mix it with the inert carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. I cannot give you an exact quantity of urea for your field.

You should use 100 kg of urea per hectare as a total, which is half the recommended rate, for the soil that has been treated with a fungicide. First, take a soil sample and have ICAT tell you the correct fertilizer dose for your field. Then spread the urea evenly, making sure it does not exceed the total recommended dose. Keep the striga-promoting fungus off the plant by not growing cotton on the same land for more than two years in a row and by planting a legume such as cowpea or soybean. I cannot give you an exact amount of urea, so ask ICAT for the specific dose for your plot.

history.content: What management steps are recommended for Striga hermonthica on sorghum?

draws.answer: The recommended action is to use a tolerant sorghum variety and cut the Striga before it germinates. Two to three weeks after sowing, three to five times per week apply urea at a rate of 100 to 150 kilograms per hectare. Then, during the flowering stage, apply the Striga spray at the labelled rate: a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel, one kilogram for about ten hectares, repeated every eight to ten days, and never apply neem powder alone. The yellowing and stunted growth in sorghum are caused by nitrogen shortage from soil that has lost organic matter. First, identify the problem by the uniform pale yellow of older leaves while the young leaves stay green, which signals nitrogen deficiency, not a disease. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a seller's recommendation, because on depleted soil mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back. Third, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: No, and you should not think about it that way because the service does not say so. Insecticides are not made stronger by mixing: mixing two active ingredients changes the composition of the product and it may no longer be what the label says. What a mix is not a stronger spray; it is a different product, and the product label carries the strength of its components, not a claim about what a mix does. Call the service, say which insect you are dealing with and what you see, and let them name the product and its rate. If you need to know the label before you mix, ANAMET is the service to ask.

No, and it is worth the trouble to know before you mix. Two or more active ingredients in a spray do not become stronger simply by being mixed: the force behind them is the solubility in water and the friction on the leaf, which depends on what is on it. If one is a water molecule and the other a gas, they do not sit together properly. That is why the label asks you to wear gloves and a mask, and why it says to mix only after you have identified the problem. And the reason the label says so is to keep the product away from children and from animals, which means fewer spills. If you have the label, read it carefully before you mix, and follow the number of days before use.

history.content: how far should fields be spaced to avoid spread

history.content: Would mixing two different insecticides give a stronger spray?

draws.answer: No, and mixing two different products does not make a "stronger" spray. The reason is the way the components interact. An insecticide is a chemical that kills insects, and its power comes from its concentration and from its mode of action. A solvent, on the other hand, is a way of carrying the product through a plant: it dissolves the outer layer so the insect inside can be reached. If two sprays were to mix, the solvent would spread itself, and the amount of each product would not be controlled. What makes a mixture stronger is not the ingredients, it is how they are combined. The right product at the right strength is the same thing, and the combination is not doubling the dose.

So if your spray has an active ingredient named "formaldehyde", you would expect to see formaldehyde on the label. Mixing two products changes the label, which is a label that says how to use it. A stronger product is the stronger kind. If it is not, do not mix, and take the product to ICAT: they can see the label first.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: This is leucaena poisoning, a nutritional issue from leucaena's high content of protein and its loss of fiber. Reduce the leucaena in the ration to only a quarter to a third, replacing it with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen gets enough roughage. Introduce the new feed gradually over several days. Always provide clean water and a mineral or salt source. If appetite does not return or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, go to the veterinary service.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that takes over the pods of sorghum, and the first step is to pull it out immediately once it appears. After removal, sow your next sorghum crop earlier, at 60-65 days, because delayed sowing raises infection risk. Use pockets spaced 80 cm apart in rows 80 cm apart, placing three grains per pocket. Sow grain with grain at a 3x3 cm depth. Apply an approved sorghum-insecticide treatment three times during flowering: first at 30-35 days when flower buds appear, second ten days later, and third ten days after that, using the labelled rate. For the exact product and dose, go to ICAT.

Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed of sorghum that you must avoid by sowing early, using close spacing and controlling the field edge weeds. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Then three to five times while the seedlings are small, applying urea at 100 to 150 kilograms per hectare, and after ten to fifteen days weed the field at two weeks and again at about thirty days. When the sorghum reaches maturity, pull any remaining Striga from the field. For details on the right variety and exact seed rate, see ICAT.
